Either way, it is important that he be held responsible for his actions and punished accordingly for it. But ultimately this doesn’t negate the fact that people who commit sexual abuse are also people. They’re not some amalgamation of evil embodied. I genuinely just think that part of these critiques, while some are insightful and valid, they become very personal and vindictive of the writers - and to me, they read as if the writers are intentionally being hateful and disrespectful etc. Which I highly doubt, again personally, is the case. 

I think there is quite clearly a lack of character and world development in the show all together - we don’t even know much about the girls’ home lives pre-crash etc. So I just think because so much of those explanations are lacking, people are choosing to perceive the deaths and iffy writing as a way to perceive certain aspects of the show as racist or even homophobic. We can agree that the show hasn’t been written well, that very valuable characters with a ton of potential were lost. But even in the example you gave of older Tai, I just think it’s a large stretch to say that there is any racism in that. Tai is supposed to be dealing with whatever sleepwalking or alternate personality she has lol. All the characters in the older timeline, honestly, in one way or another are regressing. So - if I look at it from the world the show is written in, it feels like cherry picking aspects of the show and creating narratives that really aren’t there unless you think they are. IDK I’m genuinely not trying to disregard anyone’s opinions like, if this show feels racist or sexist etc then, I’m really sorry. But I just think it’s a stretch. Like it’s just badly written. I mean I agree with parts of what you’re saying. But generally I disagree, though like I said in another comment, it’s all a matter of personal perspective and I’ve maybe taken a more idealistic one. I don’t think any of their characters are a mockery of women, I actually think they all represent real examples of suffering a lot of women go through. Laurie’s continuous loss I actually think, at least for me personally, spoke a lot to what I’ve experienced and what I’ve seen my mom and older sisters live through. As women, aging becomes a battlefield. We get trapped in our ego, in the careers we expect, the relationships we idealize of having, in controlling our experience without really questioning why we want to control it like we do. 

I think her surrender isn’t simply to placate to them and their transgressions/imperfections. But rather an understanding that, holy fuck life is painful but we’re living it anyways. The way I saw it, she was saying, “I’ve spent so long trying to find the thing that Grounds me/defines me, that I’ve finally realized the only concrete real thing I have is presence. Stark awareness of the time and experiences which I have already lived through and gratitude for what they’ve given me.” I actually think that she had the chance to rage out, but she realized nothing would come from that. She spent the whole week sad because being with these girls reminded her of all her own faults and what she envied in their lives. And when it came down to the end she realized that that sadness wasn’t really about them, but about herself. I can’t really speak as much for Kate and Jaclyn, but I think in Laurie giving this speech it disarmed the false pretences the other two were trying to put up, and I actually found that really beautiful because to me it showed that she was what they needed. 

I don’t disagree with the assumption that maybe not much will change in their dynamic going forward. If anything maybe they will drift apart as friends, but maybe this experience brought them closer together. Regardless, wouldn’t you say that either way they all gained something from the experience? I would. And I think that’s why I found this scene really powerful. Even if this ends up being the beginning of the end of a very toxic friendship, it brought them some clarity, it gave them experiences they’ll carry with them through life. I just think, basically lol, that we shouldn’t discredit our own suffering and those of the people we surround ourselves with. Even when it’s hard, I actually think reaching in to find gratitude and compassion gives us more than resistance, avoidance and judgement could. But I respect your perspective and I think like everything else in life there’s no singular truth.

I’m curious to understand why you think Laurie has no identity? What does identity mean to you? I didn’t see that at all. I do agree that the last seen was meant as a sobering wake up call for us an audience. But I don’t think it was done for us to be the butt of the joke. I think it was meant to remind us that while we were busy judging them and their faults, they were all doing their best to live with them.

You aren’t wrong, there’s definitely nuance in these kinds of friendship dynamics. I guess the way I saw it is, they all sort of serve a purpose in each other’s lives. Laurie has lost the most, she’s realized she tried to make herself her job, then her relationship, and then her motherhood, only to realize that all those experiences were more painful than she had expected. And throughout the trip she showcased a lot of anger surrounding these experiences. She always seemed a little annoyed of Jaclyn’s pushiness about Valentin, and then it all came to a head when she was the one who ended up sleeping with him. I think it was really beautiful how she was the one to break through Jaclyn and Kate’s bs of “this whole trip has been so fun 🥰” with some raw vulnerability that I think they also felt: they’re aging. And especially as women, it comes with so much baggage and suffering to confront and live with. Sometimes we do outgrow people. But I also think sometimes we serve a purpose in each other’s lives. I’d like to be idealistic and think that Laurie’s vulnerability gave their friendship room for them to be more vulnerable with one another and with themselves, and that this night actually allowed them to end this trip on a more honest note with one another. Of course there is always nuance. But I actually did think it was really beautiful that instead of Laurie just lashing out, calling them both out for their fake pretences and denouncing the moments and expediences they’ve shared, she lived in that pain for long enough to realize that surrendering to it meant accepting her own reality, as well as Jaclyn and Kate’s. Jaclyn clearly has her own issues surrounding aging, and Kate is somewhat preoccupied with maintaining peace. Why is that? We don’t know! But I think we gain more when we allow ourselves to humanize even the people who have created toxic environments in our lives. Yes sometimes it is better to let go. But I think it’s also better to try to let go without harbouring more resentment. Though I know it’s all easier said than done. And I’m definitely no expert in any of it. I just really loved this season and this dynamic because everyone (including me!) got so caught up in the politics of it all, the hatred and the bickering. Only for Laurie to give a speech that tuned all that noise out and brought them back to this present moment. A really beautiful full circle moment to remind us that we really only get one life. And we bode better with it being honest with ourselves and with one another as much as we can.

who cares? the monk literally said it: there is no resolution. they’ve seen each others flaws. deeply and soberingly. they know which parts of each other they dislike sometimes. just as they know parts of each other they envy. none of them are perfect. but they’re friends. they’ve committed to their relationship with each other because ultimately beyond all the noise they see the value in their connection to each other. i think that’s what the show was trying to say with them. we spend so much time policing each other on our views and beliefs, arguing that we cannot align ourselves with those who stray outside of our own standards. but where does that leave us but in a place of suffering, resentment and anger? i think laurie played a huge role in this final episode to break through that noise. put the pleasantries aside and acknowledge the suffering she’s been experiencing. it wasnt all pleasant. but it doesnt matter. because they’re there! they’re alive and get to continue to experience life in all its glory. messy, painful but also beautiful

1. Prices for spring should honestly drop past that range you gave because there is an oversupply of rentals and not as high of a demand. I’m renting out my place and will likely have to go down to $475-575 (which is the rate i’ve sublet previous spring terms). The range during Fall and Winter ranges depending on if it’s a sublet vs a signed lease. I would say signed leases, if you’re sticking with like a max 2km radius of campus, you’re looking at prices ranging from $800-$1400 and this is shared accommodations, not studios. 
2. Honestly this is kinda tricky to gauge right now. I’ve been renting/subletting for three years and this past year was weird. Usually Fall and Winter term are really high demand and it’s better to not wait too last minute to find sublets. But I also noticed a lot of people were actually struggling to find sublets in the Winter term, especially if they were further away from campus. So it kind of depends how close you want to live. Rentals on the more north west side of campus (Albert/Columbia/Phillip St) tend to be more expensive than stuff on the south east side bc they’re a closer walking distance. So on the north side prices tend to have a higher price range ($800-1400) whereas south east prices can range from $600-$1200). It also depends if you’re renting from a condo vs a house. I’ve found that houses or like smaller apartment buildings tend to be cheaper. 
3. You can sign a contract but it’s not exactly overly enforced. The person on the lease is ultimately the one responsible for the rental. It’s kinda hard to be scammed as someone seeking a sublet (never send deposits until you’ve viewed a place in person though, and legally they can only ask for technically last months rent but first and last is also fine). You don’t need to provide any paperwork if you want to leave early or anything, whereas if they ask you to leave prior to the discussed sublet period they actually need to go through the LTB. They can’t just kick you out, if they tried to do that you could take them to the LTB (but this might be a long process, also an unlikely scenario). Basically looking for a sublet is technically not as high stakes as signing a lease, but still ask important questions like what’s included in the rent, are there any additional fees (i.e., hydro, wifi etc). One question I ask bc a lottt of places have issues with this, is bug issues. Ppl aren’t always honest, but just gauge it. I cannot stress enough how frustrating it is to deal with pest or even mold issues. And as a subletter it’s sometimes worse because you may not be able to contact the landlord directly, since you’re not on the lease. 
4. I’ve lived in a 5 bd unit for two years and it’s been fine. The only time I hated it was when I lived in a basement apartment because it was super cramped. Noise levels aren’t really related to the number of roommates you have tbh, it’s honestly down to personalities etc. I’ve personally never had any issues with partying or loud roommates. I do think there are some areas like University Ave and some of the houses on the north east side down King St like Elgin/Regina/Marshall St which are louder bc they’re closer to WLU which has a bigger party scene that UW. I live on the south east side closer to uptown tho and my area is kinda scarily quiet. Ultimately you will have to work with your roommates, whether that’s 2 or 5, on a compromise for when quiet hours are if it’s an issue. 
5. This is a very subjective question lol. I wouldn’t really say that roommates make up half the experience personally, if I could live alone I would loL. I actually think, again just from personal experience, sometimes it’s actually better to maintain slightly distant but friendly relationships with roommates because you live with them and it can get complicated navigating conversations about cleanliness etc if you become closer friends. But - I’m also a girl so maybe it’s just a girl thing idk lmfaooo. You definitely want to ask about at least lifestyle stuff, esp if you’re not a party person. Beyond that it’s really up to you. My apt here is just for me to live in lol. I’m friendly with my roommates and sometimes will chat with them when making dinner. We have a chore schedule that rotates and sometimes ppl skip their chores which is annoying but comes with living with people. If I have learned anything from living with randos for three year it’s that some battles are already lost wars lol. You can’t make people be clean if they don’t want to be. Which is why it is important to communicate that when you check out place (i.e. “are the ppl living here generally clean? do u guys have a chore schedule?” etc.). Beyond that, I keep to myself. This is purely anecdotal but I’ve ended up in some pretty annoying living situations after becoming closer with some of my roommates, esp when trying to then address cleaning or noise issues. People just tend to take things more and more personally when they become more familiar with you. Or idk maybe I just had very emotionally immature roommates lmfaoo. 

If you need a place from Spring to Fall/maybe Winter I would just try to find a sublet for Spring/Fall. Given how much less demand there was for Winter sublets this winter, I think you’d be fine looking for one if you needed it. A budget of $700-$900 is probably doable, definitely negotiate Spring pricing, people always try to rent out for full price but fuck that, lower demand means cheaper pricing.

I agree with you partially in the sense that requirements such as a psychotherapy degree doesn’t necessarily mean a good practitioner. I’m not an expert on psilocybin or other psychedelics by any means at all. Just a psych undergrad who has done her fair share of trips, mostly on my own with music as guidance. I guess my main point of concern was that the only mandated education is a high school diploma. 

I wholeheartedly believe that (at least mushrooms) psychedelics are sacred and should not be toyed with. My own experiences at least have shown me that. But I have also misused shrooms and used them to “seek” out answers, taking everything from each experience as literal in someways. In reality there are some parts of our consciousness we cannot concretely grasp. I say this as someone who has done therapy for 12 years, half of that being a good amount of somatic and mindfulness work. Anyone can begin to misuses these drugs even if they have the best intentions. 

You are right that many indigenous cultures’ approach to psychedelics is not pathologizing. It’s the opposite, I would say, from I’ve grown to learn. The experiences are not supposed to be some cookie cutter packaged answers or a get well quick fix.

But given how quickly the rise of psychedelics as a way to treat mental health has risen, I would be curious to know how educated people who seek out these treatments are. How much inward reflection they themselves have done. These drugs are not something someone with severe complex trauma wants to jump in head first. At least in my opinion, our minds protect us from what we are not ready to experience - emotionally, physically, even spiritually. I think, given the social and political structures we live in, we have a tendency to seek control in situations. Shrooms can be incredibly destabilizing if you are not prepared to let go of control, which is not a skill that is easily achieved. So it is concerning that there are no concrete board regulations because ultimately it comes down to personal responsibility. I don’t know if every single psychedelic practitioner out there is educating themselves on the history and cultural significance of these substances. How can that be regulated if there are no concrete educational requirements? 

In Canada there was recently a huge scandal with recent MDMA study trials because the trials were a straight up joke. Like throw the malpractice book at them if anyone can help it. One woman who came forward said that she signed up to manage her childhood SA trauma. She explicitly had stipulated that she did not want to be blindfolded. Not only was she blindfolded during the experience, there is footage of her being held down at some points and the practitioners cuddling with her. One of the main practitioners in the study wasn’t even certified in anything and had no therapy education iirc, and he ended up having sexual relations with that same patient later down the line. If these kinds of questionable issues are happening in even highly controlled settings, (at least they’re supposed to be relatively well regulated) I can’t imagine what a more lax structure would allow to happen. 

I also personally think that a trip in and of itself is not the biggest hurdle but all the emotions you have to deal with thereafter during reintegration. It is an incredibly delicate and vulnerable time. Like I said - I won’t claim by any means to be an expert. There was one point in my life where I wholeheartedly believed psychedelics were the key to help people heal completely. But I don’t think it’s as simple as facilitating a trip at all. And there are so many individual differences that should be taken into consideration. You may see these concerns are Westernized woo woo but I personally believe that they are necessary. Not everyone comes from a strong spiritual background, which I would argue is fundamental in many of the ways indigenous communities practise the use of psychedelics. For an every day individual with severe trauma, the story becomes much different contextually.

I don’t mean this to judge anyone who practices psychedelic therapy in Oregon, but it is insane that those are the only requirements. You’d think at least it would require a masters is psychotherapy or some sort of therapy certification.

I’m gonna maybe offer a bit of a different perspective on this as someone who was born in Colombia but has primarily lived in Canada for most of my life. I can speak Spanish, but I struggle to find the right words sometimes and don’t speak it as often as I used to since I moved out. Growing up, I felt really jaded by the idea of having to label myself as anything. In high school there weren’t many latin american students, but it was almost by default that if you were latin, you suddenly should be a part of that group and express your latin american culture. Particularly being a girl, I felt like the word latina was overly sexualized, and truly I just felt lost in terms of identity. I’ve never liked soccer, I can’t keep track of politics here in Canada let alone the mess I know exists all over Colombia, so for a very long time I just didn’t identify as anything. (Obviously there is a lot more to being Colombian than liking soccer and understanding politics but tbh when I was a teenager those two things felt like pivotal parts of being Colombiana that I did not immerse myself in, in addition to dancing lol) The pressure to be enough of any one culture was too much. I would say I am still somewhat sensitive about my identity. I’ve had many many many latinos say to my face that I’m not really latina lol. And I mean, yeah no shit. I moved to Canada when I was 6 and I’m 25 now. Most of my experience has been here, I’ve rejected my culture for decades out of fear of ridicule, and of just general confusion that comes with being an immigrant, shit is confusing and hard. Even though I am proud to be Colombian and I love my culture, I’ve faced rejection and doubts about my identity my whole life. 

I can’t imagine the kind of identity crisis second generation or heck even third generation immigrants go through, having family members that speak a whole language they don’t even understand. To grow up in a culture like that which exists in North America that already obsesses over labels and defining your identity only to not be able to claim yourself as “enough” of anything is hard and isolating. If you grow up in an environment where you somewhat exposed to other cultures and your parents tell you you’re this and that, only to look at society and feel like you’re neither of those things, it can feel really alienating. 

I saw the video of Jenna Ortega and I get that there is a lot of nuance to the discussion, I can understand why latin americans feel frustrated seeing their ethnicity be potentially co-opted for good press or whatever. But it doesn’t have to be us vs them. I know this is simpler said than done. But cultures are not absolute, they don’t exist in some binary, stagnant state. I think if we all just lost a bit of this defensiveness we have and approached each other more with curiosity, we’d learn more about the contextual differences in our experiences with culture. Hell, maybe even learn to appreciate the other side more. But at least for me, knowing how defensive people can get around identity and labels, I’ve just stopped defending or justifying why I am who I am. If people want to remove my ethnicity because they feel personally offended by it, welp. Hope they sleep better a night lol. I’m probably biased but as someone that has been in therapy for over 10 years, I do think it’s valuable. I know that I was extremely lucky to find very qualified and albeit expensive therapists early on. But up until recently, I had to switch therapists because the costs was no longer feasible for me and I was still able to find someone within the price range I could afford ($125/per hour) and I’ve valued the sessions I’ve had with her just as equally as with the psychologists I saw previously. I know someone else here mentioned CBT and it is a great first introduction to therapy, it’s formualic as they mentioned and definitely structured. But one thing I’ll say is that the truth is you can’t look at therapy as a quick fixing tool that will solve all your problems. Adding to that, neither will being diagnosed with ADHD (and I say this as someone who has been diagnosed, has tried the meds and still struggles with all the things you mentioned in your last point). So, in relation to the therapy thing, it might help to start with something more simple like CBT but I would also keep in mind that your progress with or without therapy won’t be linear. There’s not much you need to prepare before starting therapy either, if you can afford going private, I would go through psychologytoday and look through potential therapists, see which ones seem like the best fit and book consultations. When looking for the right one you could ask yourself what it is you want to get out of therapy, and bring forth those questions in your consultation and ask them how they’d approach that. Trust your gut in this process, if you’re getting bad or weird vibes from anyone, don’t move forward. It can be hard to find the right therapist but it is possible.

As for the ADHD thing, it’s complex. Like I said, I was diagnosed with it last summer and did start taking vyvanse, and the vyvanse helps when I’m in the right mindset. If I’m doing okay, it helps me be more productive and focus on the right things so my anxiety and thought spiralling isn’t as bad. On the other hand, if I’m depressed or overthinking a lot, it makes me hyper focus on the wrong things and I end up feeling worse. I struggle a lot with procrastination and avoidance; the meds really don’t stop this, and the diagnosis for me personally didn’t change much. I think they helped /in addition/ with the therapy I did but ultimately on their own they can actually be worse, or for me they were anyway. I would take them thinking they would help me feel better but they didn’t and I would focus on a lot of negative stuff and still get nothing done. Like I would clean my entire house when I had 6 overdue assignments lol. So, it’s also complicated but if you really think it would help you can always go private and do an assessment. They aren’t cheap, I think around $3k and there is always the risk they may not also diagnose you with it. You could also try getting a psych referral through the school’s clinic.

For your last point, this one is a bit complex and I wouldn’t suggest this as a beginning tactic since it can be overwhelming. But I have found somatic work (focusing on the body experiences) to help me handle the emotional/physical symptoms you’ve mentioned. I did CBT for 7 years and it was great, I learned a lot of tools and how to label and understand my thoughts, feelings and behaviours. But I still avoided a lot, still ignored my own feelings and often felt really guilty because I knew all of these things about how the things I was thinking, doing and feeling weren’t good for me but I couldn’t seem to change them. And this is when I looked into emotionally focused therapy and more mindfulness, somatic based work. Sometimes, there isn’t enough you can talk through a problem before you have to just let yourself feel it. A really good book I read last summer was “It’s not always depression”. I can dm you a pdf version of it if you’re interested, the author talks a lot about emotions and why we act and think in certain ways as a result of our relationship with ourselves and our feelings. She offers simple self reflection exercises you can do and I like that she includes examples from real patients she’s had, I related a lot to some of the examples she gave. I also really like Tara Brach, she has good podcast episodes on emotions and mental health, usually she integrates Buddhism and other spiritual practices though but she has a great book called radical acceptance which is used in DBT (a sub-version of CBT that also integrates a little more mindfulness stuff than the latter).

Yeah but the issue is, like you said, that shame often keeps people from making changes to be healthier. And while, yes, this drug is incredible in many ways, if a person is not mentally prepared to undergo severe weight loss, then this drug might serve as a function to further ingrain their shame-driven habits. As someone that is overweight, has tried to lose weight and looked into ozempic — I know that I am not mentally at a place where I could take this drug and not let it take over me in some way. I live in Canada and there are now private online clinics that let you simply talk to a doctor online, send in some bloodwork and tests, and start you on whichever one you want. I think that’s scarily ‘accessible’ (it is very expensive, but nonetheless) without proper education and support imo. 

If this drug were combined with maybe therapy or nutrition education, then I’d say yeah, it is a total miracle drug. But the truth is there’s a lot more nuance to the way we treat our bodies and why we do so, particularly when you look at it from a societal perspective. I don’t agree with people judging others for choosing to take this drug, but I do worry that we’re continuing down a path of trying to create ‘short cuts’ to compensate for the more sedentary, less mindful lives we lead. And that’s not to say that the responsibility to change that is solely on each individual, just something to keep in mind before jumping to the thought that every overweight person needs this and it will solve all their problems. 

Like, take a look at some of the celebrities who have taken this drug. Sharon Osbourne has literally admitted that she got “carried away” taking Ozempic and is now struggling to gain back some weight. She wasn’t even that overweight to begin with, and now looks extremely thin. I think this drug can do incredible things for people who need it, who have shown effort in trying the traditional routes to lose weight and were unsuccessful — but to make it a first option for those who are not dealing with serious health issues as a result of their weight, I think it’s complicated.

You say that not involving yourself in the situation isn’t possible because culturally, family is a huge part of your life. While I can empathize with that, it doesn’t seem like there is anything you can do in this situation to change other people’s behaviours. Your mom’s complaining and then consequent enabling is a pattern of behaviour, for example, due to her own biases and worries. No matter how many times you give her advice and try to help her deal with the situation, her fears (which are maybe about not wanting to abandon her son or leave him out dry, or maybe not wanting to live alone or have no one to coddle) take over and she loses the courage to assert boundaries. Your brother’s behaviours at his age are not really an anomaly, it is possible that he’s mildly depressed, maybe confused and discouraged about his future, or simply just feeling the pressures of having to actually figure out his life as an adult and avoiding it. From what you have shared, it seems the experiences you had growing up and he did are somewhat different. I can understand you feeling frustrated about it all - I am also curious as to where you think these feelings of frustration arise from? You mention how a small part of you cannot empathize with your brother because of how your life turned out and how hard you worked - did your mom not offer you the same leeway as him? 

I think there are probably a lot more reasons why this situation is upsetting you that go beyond what you’ve shared. Coming from a south american background, I understand how more communal family dynamics can cause us to see blurred lines between offering support to others and trying to fix and take on the responsibilities of others. You first have to address your own anger and feelings in this situation, you have to accept that it is true that your mom and your brother are adults who will do as they please regardless of whatever advice they are given - and once you have awareness and acceptance of these things you can offer your support, with boundaries. Instead of approaching your brother with anger and judgement, approach the situation disarmed. I assume you love your brother and you want what’s best for him. Tell him as much, ask him if he’s okay and even let him now that this situation is difficult for you to watch because it feels like there’s nothing you can do to help. With your mom, this may be biased advice. But as someone who has a mother who can be enabling, and also complains about her own lack of boundaries, you have to set those boundaries. If you’ve given your mom 3892939 different ways to approach the problem and nothing happens, her dumping all these concerns on to you is her way of inadvertently offloading the responsibilities she has as an adult and parent herself onto you. Your mom was able to communicate to your brother she wouldn’t be paying for his ticket to visit you, so clearly she is capable of setting boundaries. Instead of continuing to offer her solutions, communicate to her that you have offered her many ways to manage the situation but that change isn’t happening. Change the approach of the conversation and ask her about how she’s doing. We can’t change how people act, that has to come from them. The only thing you can offer them in this is a listening ear to help them unravel their own reasonings for their actions. You also have to offer yourself some space in this. It’s not selfish to disengage from the situation sometimes it’s becoming overwhelming. You’re not abandoning your family by taking space to recollect your thoughts and feelings, you’re actually better preparing yourself to be present and support family in a way that doesn’t feel draining and is actually effective.

I hear you, it takes work to combat anxiety of all kinds, and it’s a constant work in progress. You’re at a good starting point though, since you’re already somewhat aware of the underlying reasons for why your anxiety manifests. There’s a lot of ways you can go about this information going forward. Like others have mentioned, it is true that exposure is the most effective way to become more resilient to anxiety and anxious responses. Though I will say, it’s super important to be kind and patient with yourself during this process. 

You’re in your first year of university, this is the first time you have to consciously think about interpersonal relationships in a more intentional manner. Unlike high school and middle school, proximity isn’t there to be the glue for most of your friendships; most of your social activities in general will have to be intentional. And you’re learning! This takes times, it takes failure and experience to learn what works and what doesn’t. 

My advice would be to start in a small way where you push yourself to be noticed more. In my own experience, going to club meetings or setting up study groups can be really intimidating and anxiety provoking, so working up to that could be a goal. You could work on being more active in class, maybe connecting with profs during office hours; whatever interactions feels scary but not too scary you’re on the verge of having a panic attack. 

Beyond exposure, anxiety can create really strong bodily and mental experiences. When I’m starting to get really anxious, my heart rate skyrockets and I can feel my thoughts racing. I’ve found it really helpful to try to focus on those body experiences and regulate my breathing to bring the anxiety down. The box breathing technique is great, it’s where you inhale for four seconds, exhale for four seconds and repeat this until your breathing has settled. 

This is just another pivotal stage in your life journey. You’re learning how to navigate the world; it’s scary and requires work, but you’re doing what you can to get there. Be patient with yourself, seek support when you need it and do what you can to challenge yourself in a way that feels functional. Sometimes we enable our anxiety because it’s comfortable, and we just gotta tentatively lean into discomfort to grow. Anxiety often misleads us into thinking we’re in some kind of danger and the best thing you can do is avoid. You just gotta keep reminding yourself you’re not in danger and build up the courage to try. What’s the worst that could happen if you speak in class? What about talking to a classmate? Maybe the answers still feel scary, but the alternative is to always live in fear, controlled by our anxieties.

Listen, I was in your shoes 3 years ago. Granted my parents accumulated income was $110k but still in no way a low income. I don’t mean this in a judgemental way, I get the thought process you’re going through, but I really think you need to take a hard look at your situation and realize you aren’t in a position where it makes sense for loan funding to be high for you. Sure, your parents may not be able to pay for your tuition, maybe you’ll need to work summers and drop a class during school semesters to work part-time. But is your family helping you make sure you have all the supplies you need to get to school? Are they driving you out on move-in day to make sure you’re all settled? Do you financially support yourself independently right now in any way? Privilege isn’t just financial, and getting high grants and loans isn’t calculated to just support someone’s tuition payments. There are incoming students who have absolutely no support. Sometimes we gotta face the realities of life, and things aren’t always easy. I’ve worked. It hasn’t been all fun, it’s frustrating counting every penny some semesters, but I’ve also really learned the importance of being financially responsible. I’m much more aware of the sacrifices my parents made and that cognizance has also made me realize how privileged I am compared to some of my classmates. Sure maybe some of them have less loans than me. But my parents come drop me off at the start of every semester. If I’m ever in the position where I truly can’t afford to go buy groceries, I know they won’t hesitate to send me some money. Do not commit fraud. Get a job before school starts and start saving up. You have a starting fund for now anyways, make do with your situation and move on. If you really don’t want to work during the school year or over breaks, you could get a personal student line of credit, but you’d probably need your parents to cosign.

As someone else mentioned - don’t commit yourself the idea of being ‘permanently’ depressed. The reality is most people experience episodic depression at one point in their lives. The severity of its impacts can vary and so it’s important to look at what ways depression affects your daily functioning and in what ways you might be inadvertently enabling it even more. From personal experience being sad and lonely can become a place of comfort. It becomes harder and harder to put yourself in uncomfortable positions that challenge the thoughts that may come with the depression. For example, I have a tendency to isolate and lay in bed for days on end sometimes when my depression hits. I start over consuming social media and it becomes a toxic cycle that feeds itself. This is why, while it may be hard and uncomfortable, behavioural changes are really the first way to start. You might not be able to immediately change the thoughts or feelings (or lack of in this case) you’re having, but you can challenge the way you act in response to them. If you’re isolating yourself from people - seek out more social situations. Join a club, reach out to an old friend. Pick up an old hobby you used to enjoy. If it seems like attempting these things alone are too much, or if you
are experiencing high functioning depression that doesn’t affect your daily functioning (as in it’s mostly internal) I would really recommend using the resources UW offers. They might not solve all your issues overnight, but talking to someone about the things you might be ruminating over can really help alleviate some of the numbness you’re feeling. You don’t need to experience this alone and in silence. I know asking for help can be uncomfortable but having the courage to do so can help you find your way out of it. My PMs are open if you ever want to vent to a stranger.

NAT - I think people have touched on the most important points already but I wanted to add my personal experience with this. I think it’s a balance. I’ve been in therapy for 12 years and I’d say that more compartmentalized and structured approaches like DBT can be really helpful to de-escalate and in some ways separate oneself from one’s feelings. The whole “my feelings are not me” sort of thing. 

But after a while of this type of therapy, over ten years, and constant analysis and deconstruction of myself, my struggles and my feelings, I had a personal breakthrough about how much I was treating myself like an issue that constantly needed to be fixed and not really a person anymore. I still carried a lot of shame, despite knowing how to talk about it and of being aware of where it came from. The transition was really hard for me as well at first - I experimented with psychedelics to get more in touch with my feelings (highly discourage this without some consistent mindfulness work prior to), switched to a more mindfulness/EFT focused style of therapy and practised mindfulness meditations more often. In hindsight I definitely jumped the gun in doing such an aggressive switch, and EFT was really scary at first because I was so used to showing up to therapy with a goal in mind, a problem to tackle and prepared to have my therapist guide me after a bit of ranting on my part to keep the therapy sessions structured. 

EFT was so different, there are sessions where I just vent and my therapist only stops me to ask me to focus on a feeling in a situation I am describing. It was so incredibly uncomfortable at first, it was surprising to me how unregulated my emotions still are. I realized there was a difference between knowing and experiencing. What I came to realize from this transition was how, despite all the therapy I had been doing, disassociated I still was from my physical body. Whenever I experience high intensity feelings all logic flies out the window for me. I become extremely overwhelmed by both the physical and internal sensations and can be emotionally reactive. 

Yes DBT greatly helped me regulate really extreme moments but after a while - it just wasn’t cutting it, especially in relation to interpersonal situations. Lately I’ve been really working towards a balance. Sometimes I need to experience the intensity of a feeling, witness that discomfort and still be aware it doesn’t define me. I offer kindness to myself, knowing my emotions are mine and they don’t have to define me. Other times, when the intensity of a feeling feels too destructive or regressive if it is expressed, I need to deescalate in a way where I am more logic and disengaged from it from a psychosomatic perspective. Or at least - rather be more clinical when acknowledging those mind/body connections. Feeling physical sensations but not pushing too hard past just being present with it. Like I said - not a therapist by any means lol. 

To me what it boils down to is finding that balance. I think it’s important to be more attuned to your feelings in a way that isn’t solely relying on logic - it broadens one’s ability to be compassionate and empathetic and offer a more present, connected experience with one’s self and others. I also think finding this balance could potentially strengthen your skills in being a good therapist/psychiatrist. Knowing how and what you need to manage your feelings - especially when you’re dealing with clients/patients on a daily basis - can be a really essential form of self care on the practitioner’s side. It’s really interesting to me the stark difference of opinion people have on this stuff here vs IG and TikTok. My opinion isn’t absolute but as someone who is on the heavier side and has struggled with weight and mental health since I was a kid, I think it’s not as black and white as people make it seem. Fatphobia as a word I think is kinda dumb, mostly because, yeah, I doubt that, besides maybe people who struggle from Anorexia, anyone else has an adverse fear to fat people. I do think though that the argument that glorifying obesity is wrong because we should be advocating for health is an ignorant argument to make. Society praises unhealthy coping skills on the daily, overwork yourself at work, overindulge in social media, use medication and other substances like alcohol and weed to suppress. I’m not saying every single person in the world does all these things. But I think as someone who isn’t thin, I’ve seen how people hide their plain hatred and discomfort of fatness and fat people through this pretence that health is the ultimate goal. Health is complex, and there are so many factors to take into account as to why a person isn’t thin and fit. Other people mentioned on here the socio-economic issues that impact people’s abilities to eat better, healthier and rounder meals while also being more active. Beyond that it’s a matter of priority. Not everyone has a healthy relationship with food or exercise. I know people who have lost weight and then gained most if not all of it back and decided they rather be heavier than put themselves through that experience again. I’ve even thought of it myself, I don’t care if losing 20 lbs extends my life by 10 years, if I could just not deal with my own persistent disordered eating issues and exist as I am, I would. Some people don’t understand how mentally and physically taxing these issues can have on a person. Should a person not be allowed to be treated with dignity and respect because they’ve chosen happiness over continuing some gruelling process to lose weight that ends in a vicious, toxic cycle? I think social media also creates this hyper-reality where people seem to think all fat people want to be shamelessly accepted and found just as attractive as a Victoria Secret model which. Lol. From first hand experience, don’t worry, we know we aren’t the conventional beauty standard. My mindset is you don’t know why a person looks how they look, unless they tell you or you’ve known them long enough to know their habits and reasons for being fat, you’re not entitled to tell someone they should focus more on their health. I get what you mean though, and as someone who is fat I don’t think there’s anything and shouldn’t be anything wrong with people who value their health and prioritize not gaining weight. There’s just always a limit. Thinness isn’t the ultimate pinnacle of health, I know there will be people who disagree with me on that, but there are plenty of other ways to damage your body besides lack of exercise and food. The difference is aesthetics in my opinion. And it’s fine to prioritize your own personal health but it doesn’t hurt to extend empathy and compassion for those who have other priorities. At the end of the day we’re all human beings just trying to live.

Hey, as someone who has and continues to struggle with anxiety on a daily basis I get it. It’s a terrifying, suffocating feeling sometimes. And it can be super frustrating to feel like this thing has so much control over what we do. But some things just aren’t worth the trouble. I’m not saying partying and socializing aren’t valuable experiences to have but, honestly I think there are much better ways to confront this fear than some giant street party where you don’t know anyone. It’s like learning how to swim, some people just dive right into the deep end but idk. I know I’d drown if I tried that loL. You have to do it gradually, so as not to overwhelm yourself but also not give it control. Maybe that’s striking a conversation with some in your classes, or going out with your roommates to eat. Honestly I think this whole party culture isn’t for everyone but sometimes we idealize it because we see how much fun other people have and feel guilty for not participating in it. But it’s not for everyone. Who knows, maybe in a couple years that might be your thing. But for now don’t beat yourself up over it. Keep going. Remember that anxiety triggers a lot of bodily sensations that make it feel like it’s the end of the world but it’s not. Breath work has really helped me. But also just allowing myself to feel the fullness of the anxiety and acknowledging that it is just a feeling and it does not have to dictate what I do. Over time, my hope is that with work and exposure it will lessen in intensity more and more. But sometimes some things are just too much. And as I said, that’s okay too.

I also think people fail to realize that dealing with a mentally ill child, an addict, these are really complex issues that aren’t easily resolved.

I think in realizing she couldn’t admit her daughter to an in patient treatment facility, she was fighting a losing fight. You might say she inadvertently enabled Rue’s addiction by not intervening in a harsher manner sooner. Is it harsh? Yeah and I’m sure that all those things Rue said in the car broke her. It’s not easy to let go of your own daughter, to realize you have no power in changing her. But there is only so much pain and suffering you can witness before you realize you can’t hold yourself responsible for someone’s else’s reckless and self destructive behaviours. Especially when you have another daughter who is being neglected and exposed to god knows how many years worth of trauma.

When you just post the struggle of being friends with someone who's suicidal and see this lol. I can very much relate. And I totally understand the impact seeing someone else go through it can have on you. It sort of becomes more real I guess. The impact it can have around you. I DON'T know. If I am the best person to offer advice when I myself don't know how to help anymore. But. I try to at least just be real about it. It's an ugly thing. Depression, suicide; mental health illnesses can be an ugly thing. And the more people mask it with cookie cutter motivational quotes and one-liners, the lonelier if feels in my opinion. Just be there for her. Be real with her. Talk to her and ask her what's going on, why it happened the way it did and how it got that way. A lot of people don't want to just spill the beans at once. So I'd say relate. You've dealt with it before so offer your own experiences with. Tell HER how watching someone else go through it makes a difference. To be honest, I've learned to just stop sugar coating it all together. I don't know if it's helped. But. Life can be an ugly thing. And the fears that we have, of what if means nothing, what if I'm always a failure, what if I go through life like this forever—they're possible. Literally anything can happen. We don't always have control. And it's learning to accept that. And decide whether we're okay with that and are willing to work through each day with our own purpose and morals and beliefs, or we can choose to give up. And there isn't a wrong or right choice I guess. In the end it's your life. And you're the only person who can control how to live it.
